hiring.text:
Rahul Venkataraman senior backend hiring debrief

We debriefed on Rahul Venkataraman's four interview rounds for senior backend. The panel agreed to move forward to reference checks, with a question about possible attrition on his last team to explore.

## Decisions

- Move Rahul Venkataraman forward to reference checks.

## Action items

- [ ] Contact the recruiter today for Rahul's reference list: two former managers and one peer (me)
- [ ] Send the meeting summary (me)

## System design

- Strong hire signal from Priya.
  - Asked about write volume first, then drew the event store partitioning scheme unprompted.
  - Handled rebalance questions well: backpressure and idempotent consumers.
  - Said when unsure, for example about a broker he hadn't run in production, and wanted to check failover semantics before committing. Priya liked this.

## First coding round

- Mixed, leaning no hire on coding, but not a hard no (Dmitri).
  - Solved the interval merge problem, but took a while and went down a wrong path for about ten minutes before correcting. He talked through his thinking aloud.
  - Did not finish the concurrent cache eviction problem. He had the structure and mostly the locking right, but ran out of time and got tangled explaining a race condition.

## Second coding round

- Lean hire (Imani).
  - Finished both problems with clean code and tests, and wrote tests before being asked.
  - Did not ask many clarifying questions and just started building. He handled one edge case Imani had planned to raise, but it was unclear whether he would have caught it without her watching.
  - Imani wants to know more about how he scopes work before a strong hire.

## Hiring manager chat

- Positive on culture and motivation (Lena).
  - Thoughtful about his current role. He wants to leave because he has done mostly maintenance on a monolith for two years and wants to build new things. Pay is not the reason.
  - Disagreed with his last manager on a rewrite and lost the argument. He accepted that but said he would have pushed harder on one part. Lena found him honest about it.
  - Mentioned team attrition almost in passing and implied he was part of why people left, then moved on quickly. Lena could not tell whether this was humility or a real issue. Priya did not see it in her round.

## Open questions

- Was Rahul part of why people left his last team? Lena and Priya think it is worth asking references directly. It is not a dealbreaker.
- Does he handle losing a technical argument well? Lena's chat suggests he does, but it is worth asking references too.

oneonone.text:
Daniela 1:1 on growth and ingestion proposal

Daniela and I talked about my wish to own design work, with a Q3 target on the event ingestion redesign that she wants to check first. We also settled that I'll draft a one-pager on the redesign by Friday and make the postmortem changes, including the rollback runbook.

## Decisions

- The postmortem's alerting gap gets its own section, not a bullet.
- I'll draft the ingestion redesign one-pager for Daniela first; she'll decide who else sees it.

## Action items

- [ ] Draft a one-pager on the ingestion redesign (problem, a couple of options, rough estimate) for Daniela by Friday; tell her if it slips to Monday (me)
- [ ] Pull the alerting gap out of the contributing factors into its own postmortem section (me)
- [ ] Add the out-of-date rollback runbook to the postmortem as an action item and update the runbook, aiming for end of next week (me)
- [ ] Ping Joaquin for the ingestion cluster throughput metrics; Daniela said he can spare about 20 minutes (me)

## Career growth

- I feel like I'm treading water: closing tickets but not growing into new work. I've been on integrations, bug fixes and the occasional migration for about eight months.
- I want to design systems, not only build what others design.
- I'd like to own a design doc end to end. My retry logic design doc last spring was a small piece of that, and Daniela said Marcus pointed to it as clean in review.
- Daniela suggested I state the goal directly, for example "I want to own X by Q3." I'm aiming for Q3 on the event ingestion redesign, which has sat in the backlog.
- Staff track: Daniela doesn't want to promise anything. It depends on how the ingestion work goes and whether I can show cross-team scope. Leading the proposal would be a strong signal. She framed it as an opportunity, not a test.

## Ingestion redesign

- Daniela wants to think about the Q3 ownership first. The redesign may overlap with Priya's team's pipeline work, so she'll check that before I dive in. Priya's team is mainly on the downstream consumers.
- The proposal is for Daniela first, written so Marcus could read it cold.
- For the estimate, rough numbers are fine. I should flag what I don't know, such as current throughput.

## Postmortem

- Daniela wants the contributing factors sharper. She said the alerting gap should be its own section, since a 40-minute delay in alerts is the most actionable finding.
- I was hesitant because the on-call setup is Dev's area. Daniela said the postmortem is about preventing the next incident, not assigning blame.

## Open questions

- Does the ingestion redesign conflict with Priya's team's work? Daniela will check and loop me in.
- Whether the Q3 ownership of the ingestion redesign is confirmed, pending that check.

brainstorm.text:
Booking app name and positioning brainstorm

The group brainstormed names and positioning for the booking app and made no decisions. Topout, Slab and Rackly are the main candidates, and trademark checks come first. We'll reconvene Thursday.

## Decisions

- No name or tagline was decided; the group agreed to sleep on it.

## Action items

- [ ] Pull trademark searches for Topout and Slab and send them round (me)
- [ ] Try taglines that don't lead with failure, avoiding lines like "never get turned away" (Tomás)
- [ ] Ask Dani's mom about the name Beta again (Dani)

## Naming candidates

- Topout: means finishing a climb and implies reaching the top; may already be a trademark (a gym management software company, possibly) and could sound like a sports drink.
- Slab: short, one syllable, a climbing word for a steep flat wall; concern that it sounds like a flooring company or a bakery.
- Rackly: friendly-sounding; someone said it sounds like a boat rental. Tomás said they like it.
- Beta: climbing jargon, but also means a software test version, which may confuse people.
- Cragline: crag plus route, but sounds like an airline.
- Belay: good for trust, but pronunciation is unclear (bee-lay or buh-lay), so it's better as a feature name (e.g. "Belay alerts", "belay queue") than the product name.
- Ruled out or parked: Access (too generic), Crux and Send (taken), Clip (common), Kit (vague and crowded), Basecamp (taken by project management software).

## Naming approach

- Should the name mention climbing? Some felt it doesn't need to, like Strava or Calm. The counterpoint was that climbing is a niche and people need to know what it is right away.
- Two audiences: gym owners pay and sign the contract, while climbers download and spread the app. The name needs to work for both.
- Core promise: "you'll actually get on the wall," which is more specific than "book."
- Avoid transport-sounding words.

## Taglines

- "Never get turned away at the door" is strong but leads with failure.
- "Book your wall" sounded like a hotel chain ad to some.

## Open questions

- Which name is the right one, Topout or Slab, pending trademark results?
- How do climbers and gym owners each react to Rackly?

sales.text:
Harbor Freight Logistics Lintly pilot scoping

The call scoped a possible six-week Lintly pilot with Harbor Freight's platform team. The pilot is tentatively set for the seventh, pending their platform lead's confirmation. Their procurement policy requires SOC 2 Type II, which Lintly won't have until October, so that is still open.

## Decisions

- Pilot with the platform team (8 to 10 people) for six weeks, warn-only for the first two weeks, then blocking on security-category findings only.
- Pre-commit secrets hook is in the pilot scope.
- The first week of the pilot counts as setup and is excluded from adoption metrics.

## Action items

- [ ] Send the Type I SOC 2 report and pen test summary to Marcus today (me)
- [ ] Check with our compliance person and auditor about a bridge letter, and follow up by Thursday (me)
- [ ] Confirm whether on-prem scoping for Enterprise is worth doing (me)
- [ ] Put a tentative hold on the seventh for pilot kickoff (me)
- [ ] Add the pre-commit hook to the pilot setup doc (me)
- [ ] Send a quote for 39 Business seats (me)
- [ ] Get approval for a pilot rate and come back with a number before Thursday (me)
- [ ] Baseline review cycle time from Jenkins and GitHub data in the first week (me)
- [ ] Send the follow-up email within the hour (me)
- [ ] Define pilot success criteria together (me and Marcus)
- [ ] Confirm the seventh as the start date and the pilot group (Marcus, with the platform lead)
- [ ] Take the security questions to legal about the Type II policy and ask whether a bridge letter is acceptable (Marcus)

## Their situation

- Around 40 engineers across the platform and routing teams, plus contractors.
- Code reviews sit for days. Median is about three days to first review, then a day or two of back-and-forth.
- Senior reviewers spend time on style, naming, unused imports and error handling instead of logic.
  - Earlier linters were turned off because of noise (about 900 warnings on day one).
- Mostly Jenkins, which times out often. The mobile driver app team uses GitHub Actions.
- Consolidating CI is a separate, open discussion on their side.

## Lintly approach

- Only enforced rules surface, ranked by severity.
- Warn-only mode annotates PRs without blocking merges.
- A baseline scan suppresses existing findings, so only issues introduced by a PR are shown. Legacy issues get worked down on their schedule.
- Plugs into both Jenkins and GitHub Actions.

## Security and compliance

- Code is analyzed in memory during scans. Only findings metadata is retained, not source code.
- Customer code is not used for model training, per terms and the DPA.
- SOC 2 Type I was completed in March. The Type II observation window runs through end of Q3, with the report expected in October.
  - Their procurement policy requires Type II for vendors with source code access. They don't yet know whether a current report plus a bridge letter would be accepted.
- On-prem deployment is Enterprise only and usually takes a few weeks to set up. Their concern is that if legal rejects SaaS-only, they're stuck.
- Their security lead wants secrets detection. Lintly's security rule pack catches common credential patterns and high-entropy strings. It can block PR merges. Local commit blocking requires the optional pre-commit hook.

## Pricing and terms

- Team is $22 per seat per month billed annually: core rules, Jenkins and Actions integrations, standard support.
- Business is $38 per seat per month: adds custom rule authoring, SSO, and audit logs.
- Enterprise is custom: adds on-prem deployment and a dedicated success manager.
- Business SSO supports SAML and SCIM with Okta, so provisioning and deprovisioning are automatic. Audit logs export to their SIEM.
- Seats are counted as active only if the developer opened or commented on a PR in the last 30 days.
  - 45 seats on Business would be about $1,710 a month, or about $20,400 a year.
  - Six of the 45 are contractors, and two are leaving at month end. Realistic count is about 39 active seats.
- They want a pilot rate, roughly half price for the first six weeks, so it's easier to approve as a line item.

## Pilot plan

- Start tentatively on the seventh. A release freeze covers prod deploys the first week of the month. Dev workflow continues.
- Success metric is review cycle time, which their VP cares most about.
- Warn-only for at least the first two weeks. Blocking on security findings only after that.

## Open questions

- Does their legal team require SOC 2 Type II specifically, or will a current report plus bridge letter be accepted?
- Will legal accept SaaS-only, or will on-prem be required?
- Is the pilot start date still the seventh, and which engineers make up the pilot group?
- What pilot rate can be approved?

planning.text:
Q1 planning sync: feature scope decisions

The group narrowed the Q1 candidates to five and agreed to make offline sync the headline, scoped to last-writer-wins with conflict copies. The AI summaries pilot was left open for the next sync.

## Decisions

- Q1 commits: template gallery, PDF export, offline sync (last-writer-wins with conflict copies), minimal permissions fix, and iOS quick-capture widget.
- Offline sync is the Q1 headline. Full CRDT merging is out for Q1 and gets revisited in Q2 if the data supports it.
- Notion and Evernote import moves to Q2, because of the Evernote nested-table export problems.
- Enterprise SSO group mapping and audit logs are out of Q1. No Q2 date is committed until the work is scoped.
- The widget ships on iOS first. Android follows later.

## Action items

- [ ] Write the offline sync spec this week, including a requirement to state the duplicate-note risk in the release notes (me)
- [ ] Confirm the offline sync scope decision with leadership, since they will ask why we're not doing full merging (me)
- [ ] Write the Notion/Evernote import deferral in the roadmap doc, with the nested-table reason (me)
- [ ] Bring AI summary cost numbers to the next sync (me)
- [ ] Block an hour Thursday afternoon to review the template gallery empty state (me)
- [ ] Finish lazy-loading for template gallery thumbnails by the 20th (Aiko)
- [ ] Design the zero-templates empty state by Thursday (Sven)
- [ ] Design the effective-permission panel, about one week (Sven)

## Template gallery

- Backend is merged behind a flag. Thumbnail lazy-loading is still needed, roughly a half-day.
- Ready for internal dogfooding this week.
- External beta target is end of January, with the 20th as the lazy-loading checkpoint.
- Sven's gallery mockups reuse the search card component. The empty state for users with zero saved templates is still unsolved.

## Offline sync

- Reading offline is mostly covered by the cache, but it's not reliable for notes not opened recently.
- The main user need is editing offline and syncing on reconnect (planes, subway).
- Full CRDT text merging: about 6–8 engineer weeks for the core, plus 3–4 weeks for mobile clients, so roughly a quarter for two engineers.
- Last-writer-wins with conflict copies: about 3–4 engineer weeks. Downside is duplicate notes when title and body are edited on different devices.
- Design: the state indicator has three options (quiet cloud icon, offline banner, per-note indicator). The conflict screen should show both versions side by side. About two weeks of design plus about a week of usability testing.
- Support data: roughly 40% of sync-related tickets last quarter were "lost my edit" or "showed the old version."

## Permissions

- Current owner/editor/viewer model confuses people about folder-shared versus direct access.
- Minimal fix: one clear effective-permission display (for example, "Jordan can edit because they're in Team Notes"). About two weeks of engineering.
- Enterprise SSO and audit logs are a separate project and were judged out of scope.
- Expect pushback from sales.

## PDF export and widget

- PDF export reuses the existing HTML styling engine. About a week, longer if font handling is difficult.
- Widget: quick capture is the more useful version, about two weeks on iOS. Android widget API is fragile, so shipping iOS first was preferred.

## AI summaries

- Me: wants a pilot, citing competitor pressure and an existing model partnership. A basic version might take about three weeks.
- Aiko: cost per user could be significant and margins are unknown. Summaries of messy notes may be poor. Wants at least a month of cost modeling and a small user test before committing engineering time.
- Sven: wants evidence of demand first. Suggested a fake summary button that leads to a waitlist to measure interest. Agreed it's a test, not a committed roadmap item.
- Not resolved whether any AI pilot engineering gets Q1 time.

## Open questions

- Should any AI summaries pilot get engineering time in Q1?
- What date, if any, can be given to sales for enterprise SSO?

customer_support.text:
Field app sync failure escalation and billing request

Marcus and Dev reported that offline jobs from field technicians are not syncing reliably to the server after the 4.11.3 rollout, and about 41 of 163 jobs were incomplete one week. I reproduced the failure on a test device and gave them an interim workaround. The sync issue is being escalated, and the billing request for their re-dispatch costs is going out today. No credit was approved and no fix date was given.

## Decisions

- Marcus's team will use the interim workaround for now: keep the app in the foreground for about 30 seconds after reconnecting, then force a manual sync from the job menu.

## Action items

- [ ] Escalate the sync failure to the sync team today, with the repro steps and the affected-region context (me)
- [ ] Send the billing request today with the re-dispatch figures, the 41 of 163 report, the repro steps and version numbers, and copy Marcus (me)
- [ ] Send Marcus a short written version of the workaround for his team (me)

## Problem and impact

- Jobs completed offline show as done on the phone, but on the dashboard they are missing, incomplete, or stuck at pending sync.
  - Sometimes the checklist syncs without photos. Sometimes photos sync but the job stays pending.
- Marcus estimates one in four offline jobs is affected, possibly more.
  - Thursday report: 41 of 163 jobs for that week were incomplete on the server. Dev confirmed the total.
- Timeline: the 4.11.3 update went out around the 8th, and complaints started around the 10th. Marcus says it has gotten worse.
- Environment: app 4.11.3 on iOS eighteen point two.
- Marcus says technicians are stuck in trucks unable to close jobs. He has about three weeks until contract renewal and is worried about how this reflects on him with his VP.

## Repro test

- Dev reproduced it on a test device: airplane mode on, create a job with checklist, two photos and signature, then airplane mode off.
  - The device showed synced, but the web dashboard had the checklist and no photos.
  - Photos were confirmed on the device, so the device appears to record correctly and the server is not receiving or is dropping the attachments.
- I said this is reproducible but I don't want to claim a root cause yet.

## Workaround

- The workaround is from other customers on this build: stay in the foreground about 30 seconds after reconnecting, then manually sync.
- On the second test job, Dev's test succeeded and the photos appeared on the web.
  - I said one success isn't proof and suggested trying a few more over the next day.
- Marcus called it a band-aid, not a product.
- If the workaround stops working or new failures appear, I suggested Marcus reply to the thread and flag it as a regression so it isn't left in the queue.

## Credit request

- Marcus estimates about $9,000 to $11,000 in labor lost to re-dispatches over the past two weeks, with technicians driving back to redo work.
  - He wants a credit on the current invoice, not a discount next year.
- I can't approve a credit or refund. Billing makes that decision, so I did not commit to an amount or outcome.
- Marcus asked who can decide and said he won't keep paying full price for an app that isn't working.

## Open questions

- Will billing approve a credit, and how much?
- What is the root cause, and when will a fix be available? No timeline was given.
- Does the workaround hold up over more jobs?

design_review.text:
# Payouts job queue move from Redis to Postgres

This design review covered moving the settlement retry queue from Redis to Postgres with SKIP LOCKED. The group agreed to proceed to a prototype once two questions are answered, and to load test before anything reaches production. Webhook fanout stays on Redis for now.

## Decisions

- Settlement retries move from Redis to Postgres using SKIP LOCKED, with polling and backoff (50 ms, capped at 500 ms when empty).
- Webhook fanout stays on Redis short term. It will be revisited after the Kafka consumer group work settles.
- Use a local idempotency table keyed on job ID, storing the processor response, instead of relying on the processor's idempotency window.

## Action items

- [ ] Pull the Redis client error logs for both eviction incident windows and post them in the doc by Thursday, March 23 (me)
- [ ] Load test the local idempotency table, target March 28 (me)
- [ ] Write up the review in the doc and tag owners (me)
- [ ] Review the pgbouncer pool config for session-level features like advisory locks (Ola)
- [ ] Check whether the Go driver uses prepared statements under transaction pooling, by March 18 (Ola)
- [ ] Confirm the processor's idempotency window with their account team (owner unclear)
- [ ] Write the decision doc on moving webhook fanout off Redis, by March 14 (Greg)

## Motivation and incidents

- Two incidents last quarter where Redis evicted keys under memory pressure and jobs were silently dropped.
- No transactional enqueue: a process crash between the Postgres commit and the Redis write can leave a ghost payout state.
- Postgres already runs with pgbouncer in front, so this adds no new stateful system. This was the main reason for the move.
- Ola questioned whether eviction was the real cause. The client may have swallowed OOM errors under the noeviction policy, which would make the fix client-side. INFO stats showed evicted_keys rising, so eviction seems real, but the client side needs checking.

## Idempotency

- The processor call happens outside the transaction: lock, mark in_progress, commit, call the processor with job ID as the idempotency key, then mark complete in a second transaction.
- The processor's idempotency window is 24 hours per the sales deck, but retries can run up to about three days. A retry after the window could double charge.
- Ola and the group preferred the local table. Storing the response also allows replaying the outcome without calling the processor again.
- Card processor retries are about 90% of volume. Internal fanout is smaller but latency sensitive.

## Throughput and latency

- Peak is about 340 payouts per second over the last month.
- The local table adds one insert and one update per job, roughly 700 extra writes per second at peak. Not load tested yet.
- Current p99 enqueue-to-dequeue is about 40 ms. Expected p99 with polling is around 120 ms, which is uncertain.
- LISTEN/NOTIFY does not work well through pgbouncer in transaction mode, so polling was chosen.

## Pooling and driver

- Transaction pooling should be fine, since each claim is a short transaction. Long holds would be a problem.
- Prepared statements under transaction pooling can cause random-looking errors. Whether the Go driver caches them is unknown. The doc may only cover the simple protocol.

## Rollback and dual-write

- Rollback plan: dual-write enqueues to both Redis and Postgres for one week while consuming from one. Rollback flips the consumer.
- Fatima raised that diverging writes could cause jobs to run twice or never run. A nightly reconciliation job compares the two sides by job ID.
- Priya's team owns the reconciler, but it is currently built for the ledger, not the queue.

## Fanout

- Options discussed were keeping fanout on Redis, moving it to Kafka later, or both.
- Two systems long term was seen as worse operationally. Adding Kafka topics right now is a concern because the consumer lag alerts have been noisy.
- Agreed to keep fanout on Redis for now and revisit once the Kafka consumer group work is done.

## Open questions

- What is the processor's actual idempotency window? The 24 hours in the sales deck is unverified.
- Does the Go driver use prepared statements under our pgbouncer pool config?
- Was eviction the real root cause, or were client errors swallowed?
- Can the nightly reconciler, built for the ledger, be used for the queue dual-write?
- What will the idempotency table load test show before production?

offsite_logistics.text:
Offsite venue, dates and budget: Porto, March 9–11

We chose Porto for the team offsite over Lisbon, mainly because the Lisbon quote was about 1,400 more and flights are shorter from Porto. Dates, budget and owners for the next steps were set, but the activity and hotel details are still open.

## Decisions

- Hold the offsite in Porto, at the converted warehouse by the river in Ribeira.
- Hold it March 9–11: Sunday arrival, Monday and Tuesday sessions, Wednesday half-day and departure, three nights.
- Budget is 1,200 euros per person, covering hotel, food, venue room and one activity. Flights are reimbursed separately.

## Action items

- [ ] Get pricing and availability for the tile painting and wine tour options by next Friday (me)

## Venue and dates

- Porto is closer for most of the team. Lisbon would add a connection for about half the people in Denver.
- The first draft said Monday to Wednesday for March 9–11. March 9 is a Sunday this year, so people will arrive Sunday night and sessions run Monday and Tuesday.

## Activity

- Tile painting seemed like a good fit for Porto and was leaned toward.

numbers.text:
Q3 close review and vendor renewals
